video_title: The Portfolio Built To Survive Every Crash | Jared Dillian
gist: Jared Dillian lays out his 'Awesome Portfolio' framework (20% each in stocks, bonds, gold, cash, real estate) as a low-drawdown alternative to 60/40 investing, then argues Fed Chair Worsh's decision to hold rates was a deliberate curve-steepening tightening move, and gives his read on the recent leveraged-fund unwind, the yen intervention, and current sector positioning (bearish financials, bullish gold, exited energy).

insights.claim: Jared Dillian's 'Awesome Portfolio' — an equal 20% split across stocks, bonds, gold, cash, and real estate — has returned about 9% a year since 1971 with a Sharpe ratio around 0.6, versus roughly 11% a year for the stock market, while carrying about half the volatility of an 80/20 stock/bond portfolio.
insights.speaker: Jared Dillian
insights.so_what: A 2-point annual return sacrifice for roughly half the volatility is a concrete, testable diversification trade-off an investor could benchmark their own allocation against.
insights.quote: the highest sharp ratio of any linear combination of asset classes I could come up with.

insights.claim: The Awesome Portfolio's worst-ever drawdown was only 12% (in 2022), its second-worst was 9% (the 2008 financial crisis), and its third-, fourth-, and fifth-worst drawdowns were each just 1% — compared with the S&P 500's 57% peak-to-trough decline from 2007 to 2009.
insights.speaker: Jared Dillian
insights.so_what: Illustrates the tail-risk case for the allocation: an investor who wants to never have to 'look at their phone' during a crash has a specific historical drawdown ceiling to point to.
insights.quote: your worst draw down ever with this portfolio was down 12% and that was in 2022.

insights.claim: Index funds like the S&P 500 are widely perceived as the 'safe, conservative' choice, but that perception is a recency-bias illusion built on 18 years of a rising market — the index has an implied vol around 16, moves roughly 1% a day, and suffered an 89% drawdown in 1929.
insights.speaker: Jared Dillian
insights.so_what: Investors treating index funds as a 'safe' default (e.g., in retirement or as an emergency allocation) are underestimating true tail risk; a large gold/cash allocation targets that mispricing.
insights.quote: there's there's nothing safe about the stock market, but since it's gone up for 18 years, everybody thinks it's actually conservative

insights.claim: A 20% cash allocation isn't purely a performance drag — it functions as an option to buy assets (e.g., real estate) cheaply when opportunities appear, and historically cash itself can be a strong asset: money market funds yielded 14-15% in the late 1970s/early 1980s (the best-performing asset in the portfolio at the time) versus roughly 4-4.5% today.
insights.speaker: Jared Dillian
insights.so_what: Reframes cash as a strategic asset with optionality value rather than dead weight, relevant to investors debating how much dry powder to hold at current 4%+ yields.
insights.quote: It's an option to buy something, right?

insights.claim: Dillian believes 60/40 and 80/20 portfolios dominate over better risk-adjusted alternatives mainly for behavioral reasons — large gold and cash allocations 'sound scary' to most investors, even though he personally finds 60-80% equity weighting scarier.
insights.speaker: Jared Dillian
insights.so_what: Suggests the resistance to diversified low-volatility portfolios is a marketing/behavioral gap rather than a performance gap, which is the explicit thesis of his new book.
insights.quote: to me 60 or 80% stocks I think is kind of scary. Like that scares me.

themes.theme: Fed Policy Under Warsh — Deliberate Curve Steepening

insights.claim: Contrary to the consensus view that Fed Chair Worsh's decision to hold rates steady was a policy mistake that spooked the bond market, Dillian believes it was fully intentional — Worsh anticipated and wanted the long end to sell off.
insights.speaker: Jared Dillian
insights.so_what: If correct, the long-end selloff isn't a credibility crisis but a policy tool, changing how traders should interpret further long-yield moves after Fed meetings.
insights.quote: I think this was completely intentional. 100% intentional.

insights.claim: A rate hike would have flattened the curve and been stimulative via lower mortgage rates, whereas holding rates steady let the long end blow out, producing an immediate tightening effect — while also giving Worsh political cover since Trump reportedly fixates on Fed funds optics rather than yield-curve mechanics.
insights.speaker: Jared Dillian
insights.so_what: Reframes 'no hike' as functionally tighter policy than a hike would have been — a nuance that matters for reading forward guidance and mortgage-sensitive sectors.
insights.quote: I don't think Trump is sophisticated enough to understand the dynamics of the yield curve.

insights.claim: Dillian expects the yield curve to keep steepening over the next 6-12 months, with Fed funds falling to around 3% while the long end stays elevated; he is personally positioned long SOFR in twos and thinks the market's pricing of roughly 1.7 hikes out to next June is wrong — he'd put the number at zero or negative.
insights.speaker: Jared Dillian
insights.so_what: A directly tradeable call (long steepener, long SOFR twos) with a specific target level (Fed funds ~3%) and an explicit view that current rate-hike pricing is mispriced.
insights.quote: we still have 1.7 hikes priced in out to June of next year. I say the number is zero

insights.claim: Worsh's broader philosophy is to shrink the Fed's role in setting rates and let the market do the work — reportedly wanting fewer FOMC meetings than the current eight — which Dillian frames as finally saying explicitly what markets already knew: the Fed follows the market, not the other way around.
insights.speaker: Jared Dillian
insights.so_what: If the Fed formally cedes more pricing power to markets, forward-rate expectations embedded in the curve become a more direct, self-fulfilling policy signal rather than just a forecast.
insights.quote: we've always kind of known that the Fed was the tail and the market was the dog.

insights.claim: A steeper curve is good for bank net interest margins, evidenced by XLF and JPMorgan trading at highs, and Dillian's rule of thumb is that a broad market correction is unlikely while banks remain strong, since financials and the wider market are usually highly correlated in selloffs.
insights.speaker: Jared Dillian
insights.so_what: Bank-sector strength (XLF, money-center bank stocks) can be used as a real-time tell for whether a broader equity correction is imminent.
insights.quote: it's kind of hard for the whole market to sell off if banks are strong.

insights.claim: The U.S. Treasury reportedly made its first outright, explicit currency intervention in roughly 30 years, selling euros in close coordination with the Bank of Japan to support the yen.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: A rare, explicit Treasury FX intervention signals monetary authorities are actively defending currency levels, a regime change worth tracking for FX and rates traders.
insights.quote: the first outright explicit move from the Treasury in something like 30 years, they they sold euros and and were closely aligned with with the BOJ.

insights.claim: Dillian views the yen as cheap on a purchasing-power-parity basis and doubts forecasts of dollar-yen reaching 250, explicitly warning against shorting yen even near 155 given Treasury Secretary Besson's track record of profiting from FX interventions, including a reported multi-billion-dollar Argentine peso trade.
insights.speaker: Jared Dillian
insights.so_what: A specific risk warning for traders considering a short-yen position: fading a well-resourced, historically successful FX interventionist is a poor risk/reward setup.
insights.quote: I just feel like being on the other side of a guy who like is a pro at FX interventions is a bad thing to do.

insights.claim: Dillian relays market veteran Dennis Gartman's rule that intervening against your own currency tends to work, while intervening to support your currency typically fails over time as FX reserves run out — though he notes Japan currently has ample reserves, which could extend how long the yen defense holds.
insights.speaker: Jared Dillian
insights.so_what: A mental model for handicapping any currency-defense intervention: check the defender's reserve depth before assuming the intervention will hold.
insights.quote: intervening against your currency always works, but intervening on behalf of your currency never does

themes.theme: The Leveraged Fund Unwind & Market Structure

insights.claim: Dillian frames the blowup of a highly leveraged fund that had grown to roughly $45 billion NAV (heavily concentrated in momentum/'meme'-style names) as a classic forced-liquidation event, with the most leveraged player getting taken out first as an early warning signal for the broader market.
insights.speaker: Jared Dillian
insights.so_what: Watching the most-crowded, most-levered positions for forced unwinds can function as an early tell for broader risk-off moves before they show up in index-level data.
insights.quote: they're the most leveraged player. They got taken out first.

insights.claim: Dillian compares the current fund liquidation to February 27, 2007, when the ABX subprime index gapped down 10 points the same day China raised reserve requirements, sending the S&P down 4% and the VIX doubling — a moment he calls the real 'starting gun' of the 2008 financial crisis even though the S&P went on to make new highs that summer.
insights.speaker: Jared Dillian
insights.so_what: A historical template for how bear markets actually begin (a sharp technical break in a 'sleepy' market, not an obvious headline crash) that he's using to interpret the current episode.
insights.quote: I I just I I look at it as the starting gun in a bare market. That's really the way I look at it.

insights.claim: In the days following the leveraged fund's liquidation, S&P price action showed essentially no intraday pullbacks and just kept climbing, which Dillian reads as a sign of real money/inflows returning rather than a mere technical bounce.
insights.speaker: Jared Dillian
insights.so_what: The absence of pullbacks in a post-liquidation rally is a tell traders can watch for to distinguish a durable inflow-driven move from a dead-cat bounce.
insights.quote: it feels like more than a bounce. It feels like real money coming in.

insights.claim: Despite recent drawdowns in momentum/meme and tech names, Dillian sees no evidence retail investors have capitulated on the belief that stocks always go up, calling the average retail trader 'indefatigable' and questioning how large a drawdown would actually be needed to break that belief.
insights.speaker: Jared Dillian
insights.so_what: Persistent retail buy-the-dip conviction after a leveraged-fund blowup suggests sentiment hasn't reset, implying more downside may be needed before a genuine capitulation low forms.
insights.quote: I think they are indehaticable.

insights.claim: Dillian is technically bearish on financials (calling the sector 'topping') while favoring defensive healthcare and staples, and frames that pairing as an implicit bearish read on the rest of the market.
insights.speaker: Jared Dillian
insights.so_what: A rotation into staples/healthcare alongside a call that financials are topping is a classic late-cycle defensive posture worth watching as a leading indicator.
insights.quote: if you like staples and healthcare, then you're generally negative on everything else.

insights.claim: Dillian liquidated his energy positions a couple of weeks before this conversation on purely technical grounds (facing pushback from readers at the time), and with oil already down $8-9 a barrel since, argues that if the Israel-Iran war episode is truly ending, oil could fall back to $60-65.
insights.speaker: Jared Dillian
insights.so_what: A specific price target ($60-65) tied to a specific catalyst (war de-escalation) for traders positioned in or against energy names.
insights.quote: here we are a week or two later and oil is like eight or nine bucks lower and you know if this really is the end of the war it's going back to 60 or 65.

insights.claim: Dillian is bullish on gold, viewing the pullback since January as a basing/bottoming process; he wants to see one more small test below $4,000 to complete the base, and considers a breakout above $4,250 a 'blue sky' signal that would send gold back toward its highs.
insights.speaker: Jared Dillian
insights.so_what: Gives traders concrete technical levels (sub-$4,000 test, $4,250 breakout) to watch for confirming or invalidating a renewed gold uptrend.
insights.quote: it's a blue sky breakout and you're going to get back to the highs at some point.

insights.claim: Lines of buyers outside physical gold shops back in January marked a clear sentiment top for the precious metals complex, illustrating how retail euphoria can flag a local high.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Physical-gold buying frenzies are a usable contrarian sentiment gauge for timing precious-metals exposure.
insights.quote: back in January, you saw people lined up outside of places to buy physical gold and that was a pretty pretty clear top.
